item.title: Data Agents Need a Map: Evolving, Demand-Driven Knowledge of Large Collections
item.description: arXiv:2611.33763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most data that could power rich analysis sits unintegrated and uncataloged in open data portals, data lakes, and collections of independently published tables. Data agents now answer analytical questions over such collections with a full workflow per question, including dataset retrieval, join discovery and evaluation, and tailored program synthesis, most of which are discarded when a new task arrives. The knowledge these workflows depend on, such as what each column means, which context a dataset leaves implicit, and how datasets combine, is therefore perpetually rederived and never persisted. We argue for persisting this knowledge in an evolving semantic atlas that users and agents can navigate and extend. The atlas describes every dataset offline, through topics, semantic types, and profiles, so that agents can find the datasets that a task requires. Relationships between datasets and integrated views, which require comparing datasets, are instead built on demand for the areas of analysis that users declare. Every item is stored with its provenance and the confidence of the methods that produced it, so that agents can decide how far to trust it or whether to abstain. As datasets change, inconsistencies are detected and corrected automatically, while human users settle what the data leaves inconclusive. We present this vision and its challenges, namely building the atlas over large, multi-domain collections, keeping it correct and up to date, serving it to users and agents, and evaluating whether it improves their answers. A proof of concept on DAB, a benchmark for data agents, shows that with only part of the atlas a coding agent can already read a fifth to a third fewer tokens while achieving the same accuracy as without it.
item.dc:creator: Christos Koutras, Yurong Liu, Laura Haas, Juliana Freire

item.title: EMMA: Efficient and Effective Cooperative Multi-Modal Analytics over Embodied AI Data
item.description: arXiv:2611.33765v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Embodied AI has seen growing real-world deployment, particularly in autonomous vehicles and robots. These vehicles and robots continuously capture large collections of multi-modal data, such as video, LiDAR point clouds, and GPS trajectories. Historical collections of these data support model improvement and safety assessment through scene retrieval, object trajectory extraction, and corresponding analysis. Processing such analytical queries is challenging because answering them may require combining information from different modalities and observations captured by different moving vehicles or robots, while extracting that information with deep models at every scene incurs prohibitive cost. We present EMMA, an operator-oriented query-processing framework for embodied AI data. EMMA compiles analytical queries into composable operators and executes them on demand. To support accurate query evaluation, EMMA performs modality-aware staged predicate evaluation and selectively combines overlapping observations. To reduce query cost, EMMA uses a temporal co-location index to identify joint-analysis candidates, adaptive scene skipping to reduce model calls, and a shared world store to reuse extracted information across operators and queries. EMMA trains execution policies offline and deploys them as plug-ins. Based on lightweight observations, these policies determine whether the current scene is analyzed independently or jointly and how many subsequent scenes can be safely skipped, balancing analytical accuracy and execution cost. Experiments show that EMMA substantially reduces query execution cost while preserving query accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Jiangneng Li, Jie Wang, Ziqi Yin, Zheng Wang, Gao Cong

item.title: Cache Replacement in Direct-Access Cloud OLAP-An Experimental Comparison and Practical Guidance
item.description: arXiv:2611.33977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct-access cloud OLAP engines rely on local caches to hide remote object-store latency, yet the replacement design space remains poorly understood. Existing systems largely inherit recency- or Clock-oriented policies from DBMS buffer management, even though cloud misses combine a size-independent request overhead with a size-dependent transfer cost and cache objects vary widely in size. We present a broad experimental comparison of 22 cache-replacement algorithms and one semantic-caching baseline across seven analytical workloads and ten cache sizes. To compare them on a common basis, we formulate Unified Hit Ratio (UHR), a latency-weighted hit ratio that decomposes into a workload-specific weighted combination of object and byte hit ratios, and equivalently, the normalized fraction of aggregate remote-download latency saved by caching. Our results yield practitioner-oriented guidance. Classical size-aware policies developed outside the DBMS literature remain surprisingly strong, dominating object hit ratio on most workloads and staying near the UHR frontier. Byte efficiency depends primarily on aggressive filtering of zero-reuse objects, while under multi-tenant drift lightweight per-request adaptation is often more robust than retraining-heavy learned methods. We instantiate these lessons in LARA, a compact reference policy that validates the guidance through competitive UHR performance.
item.dc:creator: Taejun Yoon, Taesung Lee, Joo Yeon Lee, Ki Hong Kim, Byungchul Tak, Wook-Shin Han

item.title: SeQLean: Verifying SQL queries using Lean
item.description: arXiv:2611.33181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present SeQLean, a system that uses formal verification in Lean to increase the accuracy of translation from natural language to SQL. This is based on modelling SQL in Lean via relational algebras. Since we do not have a translation known to be correct, we cannot directly prove correctness. Instead, we use proof challenges: tests of internal consistency that are unlikely to be satisfied by an incorrect translation. The simplest proof challenge is based on generating two translations of the same natural language query into SQL, ideally with one being optimized for performance and the other for understandability. If two translations are equivalent, they must give the same answer for every database. This can be checked using proof automation in Lean. Using Lean allows us to have essentially arbitrary properties as proof challenges, and also check these (including equivalence) taking into account known properties of the underlying database system. Even for equivalence queries of an arithmetic nature, we show that Lean can be more powerful than traditional tools due to the availability of Mathlib theorems. A JSON API over HTTP allows the verifier to be integrated into agentic frameworks.
item.dc:creator: Siddhartha Gadgil, Anirudh Gupta, Ajay Kumar Nair

item.title: First-Class Relationships as a Representation Threshold: Identity, Time, Confidence, and Causation
item.description: arXiv:2603.13603v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Operational records -- who may access what, what changed, what caused an incident -- consist of relationships that involve several parties, hold for a period, are believed with some confidence, and cause one another. We ask what a representation must provide to store such records directly. We state four storage requirements: n-ary relationships with attributes, temporal validity, confidence with an evidential basis, and causal links between relationships. Under our definitions, each requires relationships to have identity: every relationship is stored, fetched and queried as an object with its own key. Confidence with an evidential basis and causal links also require composition: any relationship can take part in another. With n-ary relationships, either one therefore requires first-class relationships, which are identified, carry attributes, and compose at every arity. Conversely, first-class relationships suffice for all four. They are thus a threshold, and it belongs to the relationship construct, not to the data model around it: where a model's own construct falls short, every representation meeting n-ary relationships together with evidence-backed confidence or causal links builds a first-class construct from other parts, as our SQL implementation does. We place SQL, property graphs, RDF 1.2 and TypeDB relative to the threshold, and present the Attributed Temporal Causal Hypergraph (ATCH), which meets all four requirements with query operators for each.
item.dc:creator: Matthew Alford

item.title: VulCPE: Context-Aware Cybersecurity Vulnerability Retrieval and Management
item.description: arXiv:2505.13895v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The dynamic landscape of cybersecurity demands precise and scalable solutions for vulnerability management in heterogeneous systems, where configuration-specific vulnerabilities are often misidentified due to inconsistent data in databases like the National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Inaccurate Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) data in NVD further leads to false positives and incomplete vulnerability retrieval. Informed by our systematic analysis of CPE and CVEdeails data, revealing more than 50% vendor name inconsistencies, we propose VulCPE, a framework that standardizes data and models configuration dependencies using a unified CPE schema (uCPE), entity recognition, relation extraction, and graph-based modeling. VulCPE achieves superior retrieval precision (0.766) and coverage (0.926) over existing tools. VulCPE ensures precise, context-aware vulnerability management, enhancing cyber resilience.
item.dc:creator: Yuning Jiang, Feiyang Shang, Freedy Tan Wei You, Huilin Wang, Chia Ren Cong, Qiaoran Meng, Nay Oo, Hoon Wei Lim, Biplab Sikdar
